Those viewpoints are missing, or covered only through older commentaries.

Main things to know:
- **Section 3 is thin.** It has no Catholic or Orthodox readings and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. The "modern scholarship" view comes from the Expositor's Bible, an older commentary on biblehub, not from the modern sites you listed.
- **Unnamed excerpts.** Some biblehub pages mix several commentators without labelling each excerpt. I don't name an author unless the page does.
- **Verses not covered:** v. 13 and vv. 24 and 28 have no separate notes. Verse 3 comes only from summaries of vv. 1–4 or 2–3.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott says the word "commandment" isn't used here. From this point Moses deals with particular institutions and requirements. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm
Gill sees a new speech beginning here. Some of these laws applied wherever Israel lived, but others belonged only to life in Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
The Pulpit Commentary says the moral exhortations end here and "positive" laws begin. These are duties that became right because God commanded them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 2:** Guzik says ancient peoples usually took over an earlier god's temple for their own god, and God refused this. Canaanite worship was largely sexualised fertility and nature worship, so its shrines sat in pleasant outdoor spots. He links this to worshipping the creature rather than the Creator (Rom 1:25). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill says the "places" included temples, which gave towns names such as Beth-peor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
Ellicott says the first requirement is to remove every trace of idolatry. This was tied to the step-by-step conquest, as work given to each tribe. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/12-2.htm
Constable says pagans thought high places brought them closer to their gods. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 3:** The Bible Hub study page says naming a hill after a god claimed the spot, so wiping out the name cancels that claim. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/deuteronomy/12.htm
The Gospel Coalition (TGC) commentary says destroying the shrines also cancels every rival claim to own the land. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/

**v. 4:** Gill reads this as "don't sacrifice to God on hills and under trees." He adds that Jewish tradition (the Targum and Maimonides) applied it to never destroying anything belonging to God's house or erasing His names. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
TGC says God's people can't adapt Canaanite worship for their own use. They must worship the way God commands. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/
Guzik applies it to people who worship the LORD *and* the things of the world. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/

**v. 5:** Guzik says the place wasn't left to Israel's feelings, and worship is a community act. He quotes Thompson's view that before the kings the sanctuary moved between Shechem, Bethel and Shiloh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill says the place isn't named, and he gives Jewish reasons for this, mainly to stop the tribes fighting over it. He identifies it with the temple at Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
The Bible Hub study page says it was Shiloh first, then Jerusalem. It points to Jeroboam's rival shrines (1 Kgs 12) as the disaster that followed. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/deuteronomy/12.htm
Constable says the rule covered public worship; Israelites could still pray anywhere. God's "name" there meant His presence in a way found nowhere else. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 6:** Guzik says the place of worship was meant for atonement, confession and giving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill reports a rabbinic rule: a vow should be brought at the next feast. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
On whose tithe this is, see section 2.

**v. 7:** Guzik quotes Morgan: worship is rejoicing that comes from being blessed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
The Pulpit Commentary deals with how this fits Num 18:18. Numbers tells the priest what he may claim, while Deuteronomy tells the people how to use what is left. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/12-7.htm

**v. 8:** Guzik and Kalland say life in the desert camp was less controlled. Guzik links the phrase to Judges 17:6 and warns against worship centred on the worshipper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill says Israel didn't ignore the law but kept it loosely, bringing offerings when and where they liked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
Matthew Henry says no society will be perfectly pure until the heavenly Canaan. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_012.cfm
Ellicott says the law of Moses has a prophetic side that recent commentators have overlooked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm

**v. 9:** Gill sees Canaan as a type (a foreshadowing) of the heavenly rest still waiting for believers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
The Precept Austin outline treats "resting place" as another name for the Promised Land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62494/

**vv. 10–11:** TGC says that once Israel had rest in the land, there would be no excuse for worship that didn't follow God's instructions. It notes Judges 21:25 as the later slide back. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/
The Pulpit homiletics argue that God waited to reveal the place, and could do so through how history unfolded. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 12:** Guzik says rejoicing is *commanded* (compare Phil 4:4) and quotes Spurgeon against dreary worship. He applies the "place" to joining God's people rather than worshipping alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill says wives aren't named because they were obviously included. The Levite shared the feast because he had no land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
A commentator quoted on this Bible Hub page says that under the gospel only Christ sanctifies the gift (Mal 1:11; John 4:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/12-12.htm
Bob Utley (bible.org) says servants and Levites were treated like extended family. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-12

**v. 14:** Gill says the tribe is left unnamed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 15:** Ellicott, Constable and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say this relaxes Lev 17:3–4. In the wilderness, animals had to be killed at the tabernacle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-12.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_012.cfm
Guzik says most slaughter in the ancient world was also a sacrifice, but here ordinary butchering isn't treated as one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
JFB says your way of living should match your means. Gill says "unclean" means someone under ceremonial uncleanness, who could still eat ordinary food. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_012.cfm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 16:** Gill says the rule covered all blood. Poured out "like water," it can't be gathered up again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
JFB traces the rule back to Gen 9:4. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_012.cfm

**vv. 17–18:** Guzik and Thompson say sacred meals belonged only at the sanctuary. Maclaren says Christ for us is our pardon, and Christ in us is our life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
The Pulpit homiletics warn that private feasting shouldn't replace public worship or the support of the Levites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html

**v. 19:** Guzik quotes Clarke: people who serve God's ministry should have their needs met. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Gill says "as long as you live" means always, not just once. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
TGC says remembering the Levite means remembering the God who gives Himself. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/

**vv. 20–22:** Gill says that in the wilderness Israel ate little meat to protect the herds, and a bigger land would allow more. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html
Ellicott says the distance to the sanctuary made this change necessary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm
Keil & Delitzsch say "alike" doesn't mean the clean and unclean have to eat together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/12-22.htm

**v. 23:** Keil & Delitzsch read "be sure" as "be strong": firmly resist the temptation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/12-23.htm
The Pulpit Commentary says the blood was the seat of life and so carried the power to atone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html
Guzik says the rule pictures all life belonging to God. He gives two explanations of the pouring out: to keep blood off pagan altars (Thompson) and to return it to the earth (Merrill). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
The Bible Hub study page links it to Acts 15:20. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/deuteronomy/12.htm

**v. 25:** Ellicott says the promise may mean physical as well as moral benefit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm

**vv. 26–27:** Gill says burnt offerings went on the altar, and their blood was poured out there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-12.html

**vv. 29–30:** JFB and Ellicott say Israel was tempted to calm the local gods out of superstitious fear. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Deu/Deu_012.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm
The Pulpit homiletics also blame curiosity driven by lust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html
Guzik warns against sinful curiosity. With Merrill, he notes that Israel kept running after gods that had already been beaten. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/

**v. 31:** Guzik connects this to Molech worship and traces its history: Solomon, Ahaz, Manasseh and finally Josiah's reform. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/
Matthew Henry says bringing pagan customs into God's worship would make the worship itself an abomination. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_012.cfm

**v. 32:** The Pulpit Commentary (citing Keil) treats this verse as a bridge into chapter 13. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html
Guzik: the standard for worship is God's word, not what people prefer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 32 (and v. 4): how strictly God's commands govern worship**
- **Reformed / Presbyterian:** Monergism puts this verse next to the Westminster Confession's rule that God may be worshipped only in ways Scripture prescribes. https://www.monergism.com/regulative-principle-worship-wcf-211
  Ligon Duncan (TGC) cites 12:32 for the "regulative principle": God alone decides the content, motive and aim of worship. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/god-teach-you-worship/
- **A looser evangelical view:** Bob Utley agrees God takes obedience seriously, but notes that Deuteronomy itself adapts the wilderness laws. He says the Bible's truths have to be applied afresh in every age. https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-12
  The Pulpit homiletics say ceremonial laws were flexible and served practical needs, unlike moral laws (for example, David eating the showbread). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html
- I couldn't reach Lutheran, Anglican or Methodist sources on this verse.

**vv. 6, 17: which tithe?**
- Ellicott says Jewish commentators take this as the "second tithe." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm
- Guzik (a Calvary Chapel pastor) says the passage only tells Israel *where* to bring the tithe. He doesn't think it adds a separate "festival tithe" on top of Numbers 18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-12/

---

## 3. Other views

**Was this centralisation law written by Moses or later? (vv. 2, 5, 13–14)**
- The Expositor's Bible says Deuteronomy's author shows no sign of knowing the tabernacle as the only place of sacrifice. It suggests the one-sanctuary rule may have grown out of Jerusalem priests' demands after the Temple was built. It also says the law aimed to end the corrupt High Places. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/deuteronomy/12.htm
- Ellicott notes that some think the command belongs to later times because early Israel didn't keep it. He argues that no later writer could have put v. 32 in Moses' mouth if he had changed Moses' laws. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/12.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary pushes back against the critics. It says the tabernacle already implied one central altar and Moses only made it plainer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/12.htm
- Constable cites a reading based on ancient treaties: Israel, like a subject nation, must pay "tribute" only to its overlord. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-12.html

**On Catholic practice (Protestant criticism only, not Catholic sources):** The Pulpit homiletics give Catholic devotion to Mary and use of images as an example of pagan worship mixed into Christianity (v. 3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-12.html
The Expositor's Bible says the Catholic distinction between worshipping God *through* an image and worshipping the image itself didn't apply in Deuteronomy's setting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/deuteronomy/12.htm
Since I couldn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, I have no Catholic or Orthodox response to put beside these.
